questions.title: How is an app in the local environment different from a deployed one, and what must an app have to work when deployed?
questions.description: Locally, the app runs on your machine with a development server (like ui5 serve or SAP Fiori tools): the files are served one by one and not minified, the UI5 framework comes from the tooling or a CDN, the OData service is reached through a proxy or replaced by a mock server, you start it with index.html, and you are the only user. Deployed, it runs on a server (an ABAP system, SAP BTP, or the SAP Fiori launchpad): it is built and minified, with preload bundles, UI5 is provided by the platform in a specific version, the real back end with real authentication and authorizations is used, it usually starts inside the launchpad as a tile (not from index.html), and many users work with it at the same time. To work in both worlds, an app must: be a Component configured through manifest.json, because the launchpad starts components, not HTML pages; use relative service URLs in the manifest's dataSources (like /sap/opu/odata/...) and no hard-coded hosts, so the platform's routing or destinations can resolve them; load all its own files relative to its namespace (sap.ui.require.toUrl), never with absolute paths; keep all texts in i18n; not depend on code in index.html; use stable IDs; handle missing authorizations and errors from the real back end; and support the launchpad features it needs, like intents for navigation and the shell's back button. Other differences: caching is off locally but aggressive when deployed (with a cache buster), errors show full stack traces locally but generic messages (with logs on the server) when deployed, and authentication is usually none locally (or basic auth in the proxy) but XSUAA / IAS or the SAP Logon session when deployed. Some bugs therefore appear only after deployment: a hard-coded localhost URL, a library missing in dependencies, a file path with the wrong case that worked on Windows but fails on Linux, or a binding that worked with friendly mock data and breaks on real data. A deploy checklist also includes: a unique sap.app.id that matches the namespace, applicationVersion, complete dependencies.libs and a minUI5Version not higher than the platform provides; launchpad integration with sap.app.crossNavigation (semantic object and action, tile title and icon); platform settings sap.platform.abap (the BSP name) or sap.platform.cf; for Cloud Foundry, xs-app.json and mta.yaml; complete i18n bundles listed in supportedLocales; no development-only code (no mock server started unconditionally, no console.log with sensitive data); security settings like frame options; and flexEnabled if the app should be adaptable.
keyPoints: Local: dev server, unminified files, proxy or mock server, index.html, one user.
Deployed: built and minified, platform-provided UI5, real back end and auth, started in the launchpad.
Needed: a manifest-configured Component, relative dataSource URLs, no hard-coded hosts or absolute paths.
Also: i18n texts, no logic in index.html, stable IDs, real error handling, launchpad intents.
Bugs that appear only after deployment: localhost URLs, missing libs, case-sensitive paths (Linux), real vs mock data.
Checklist: unique sap.app.id, crossNavigation inbounds, sap.platform.abap/cf, xs-app.json + mta.yaml, no dev-only code.

questions.title: Which approaches exist for building web apps: Grunt, Gulp, SAP's internal tools, and the UI5 tooling?
questions.description: Building means turning the source code into an optimized version for deployment: minifying JavaScript (and keeping -dbg.js copies), creating preload bundles, compiling themes, converting TypeScript, and copying everything into a dist folder. Several generations of tools have been used for UI5 apps. Grunt and Gulp are general JavaScript task runners: Grunt works with configured tasks, Gulp with code-based streams; for UI5 there were plugins (like grunt-openui5) to create preloads and themes. They were common in older UI5 projects, but are no longer the recommended way. Inside SAP, teams also used internal build and tooling solutions (like the SAP IBSO SAPUI5 Tools mentioned in some internal guidelines); these are company-internal, documented in internal wikis, and not available publicly. The current standard is the UI5 tooling (UI5 CLI, @ui5/cli), an open-source, UI5-specific tool from SAP: configured with a ui5.yaml file, it serves the app locally (ui5 serve) and builds it (ui5 build) with all UI5-specific steps built in, understands the dependencies to UI5 libraries, and can be extended with custom tasks and middleware. SAP Fiori tools build on top of it. Other general tools, like npm scripts, are used to call it. The answer a reviewer wants: "Grunt, Gulp and the IBSO tools are the previous generation. UI5 Tooling replaced them and is the standard now. I would only meet the old ones in a legacy project, and migrating to UI5 Tooling would be my recommendation."
keyPoints: Building: minify, create preload bundles, compile themes, transpile TypeScript, write dist/.
Grunt and Gulp: general task runners with UI5 plugins; used in older projects.
SAP-internal build tools (like IBSO SAPUI5 Tools) exist inside SAP, documented internally only.
Current standard: the open-source UI5 tooling (ui5.yaml, ui5 serve, ui5 build), used by SAP Fiori tools.
Say it clearly: Grunt/Gulp/IBSO are legacy; UI5 Tooling is the standard; migrate legacy projects.

examples.title: Building with the UI5 tooling
examples.code:
npm install --save-dev @ui5/cli

npx ui5 serve              # local development server
npx ui5 build --clean-dest # optimized build into ./dist
npx ui5 build --all        # also build the dependencies (libraries)

examples.title: UI5 Tooling commands
examples.code:
npm install --save-dev @ui5/cli
ui5 serve                  # development server
ui5 serve --open index.html
ui5 build                  # production build into dist/
ui5 build --all            # also build the framework dependencies
ui5 build self-contained   # bundle the used UI5 parts into the app

questions.title: What is a Component-preload file?
questions.description: Without bundling, an app would load each of its files separately: Component.js, manifest.json, every controller, every view, every fragment, every formatter. That can easily be dozens of HTTP requests before the first screen appears. Component-preload.js is a single file, created during the build, that contains all of the app's modules and resources (JavaScript modules, XML views, fragments, and other resources) in one bundle, already minified. When UI5 creates the component (asynchronously), it first loads Component-preload.js and registers all the modules in it, so later, when the app needs a controller or a view, it is already available without a request. This makes startup much faster, especially on slow networks or with high latency. It is created automatically by the UI5 tooling (task generateComponentPreload); libraries get a similar library-preload.js. Because the deployed app uses the preload, changes to single source files on the server are not visible until the preload is rebuilt; for debugging, the URL parameter sap-ui-xx-componentPreload=off makes UI5 load the individual files instead. The original files are still deployed beside it: UI5 uses the preload, and anything not in it is fetched individually; -dbg versions are generated too, so a deployed app can still be debugged (sap-ui-debug=true). Why it matters so much: on a slow or high-latency connection, the number of requests dominates loading time far more than file size, so this single file is usually the biggest startup improvement available.
keyPoints: Component-preload.js bundles all of the app's modules and resources into one minified file.
UI5 loads it first when creating the component, so later module requests are avoided.
It makes startup much faster; created by the build (generateComponentPreload); libraries have library-preload.js.
sap-ui-xx-componentPreload=off loads single files instead, for debugging.
Request count beats file size on high-latency networks: the preload is the biggest startup win.

questions.title: What are the main features of the UI5 tooling: its main tasks and build types?
questions.description: The UI5 tooling is configured per project with ui5.yaml: the specVersion, the project's metadata.name, its type (application, library, theme-library, or module), the framework (OpenUI5 or SAPUI5, with a version and the libraries to use), and optional builder and server settings. ui5 serve starts a development server with live module serving, and ui5 build creates the optimized result in dist. The build runs a standard list of tasks, in a fixed order, for example: replaceCopyright and replaceVersion (fill placeholders), minify (minifies JavaScript, creates the -dbg.js files and source maps), generateFlexChangesBundle (bundles UI flexibility changes), generateComponentPreload for applications (or generateLibraryPreload for libraries), buildThemes for libraries (compiles LESS into CSS), and generateVersionInfo. Some tasks are optional, like generateCachebusterInfo, and can be included or excluded with --include-task and --exclude-task. Build types: the default build creates the preload bundles; ui5 build self-contained creates a standalone app with one custom bundle that also contains the needed parts of UI5 itself (no external UI5 needed); ui5 build jsdoc generates API documentation. Options like --all (also build dependencies) and --clean-dest are common. More tasks worth recognizing: generateVersionInfo (writes sap-ui-version.json), generateCachebusterInfo (the cache-buster index), and generateResourcesJson (the resource index). The distinction that matters for build types: a normal ui5 build is right for ABAP and SAP BTP, where UI5 is already provided by the platform; self-contained is for standalone hosting on any static web server, but it makes the app much larger and pins it to one UI5 version, so it is the exception. Common middlewares in a real project: a proxy (fiori-tools-proxy or ui5-middleware-simpleproxy) to avoid CORS, ui5-tooling-transpile for TypeScript, ui5-middleware-livereload, and @sap-ux/ui5-middleware-fe-mockserver for OData V4 mock data.
keyPoints: ui5.yaml: specVersion, metadata.name, type (application, library...), framework + libraries, builder, server.
ui5 serve for development; ui5 build writes dist.
Standard tasks: replaceCopyright/Version, minify, generateFlexChangesBundle, generateComponentPreload, buildThemes...
Build types: default (preload), self-contained (bundles UI5 too), jsdoc; --include-task / --exclude-task / --all.
Default build for ABAP/BTP (platform provides UI5); self-contained only for static hosting (large, pinned version).
Common middlewares: fiori-tools-proxy, ui5-tooling-transpile, livereload, fe-mockserver.

examples.title: ui5.yaml of an application
examples.code:
specVersion: "4.0"
metadata:
  name: my.app
type: application
framework:
  name: SAPUI5
  version: "1.120.15"
  libraries:
    - name: sap.m
    - name: sap.ui.core
    - name: themelib_sap_horizon
builder:
  resources:
    excludes:
      - "/test/**"

questions.title: How do you implement a custom middleware (and custom task) for the UI5 tooling?
questions.description: The UI5 tooling can be extended with your own code. A custom middleware runs inside the development server (ui5 serve), on every request: it can answer requests itself, change them, or pass them on. Typical uses are a proxy to a back end, live reload, serving mock data, or adding headers. A custom task runs during ui5 build, and can create, change or remove files, for example transpiling, generating a file, or replacing placeholders. Both follow the same pattern. First, the extension is declared with kind: extension and type: server-middleware (or task), a metadata.name, and the path to its implementation, either in the project's ui5.yaml (separated by ---) or in an npm package. Second, the implementation is a module that exports a function. For a middleware, this function receives an object with log, options (including options.configuration from ui5.yaml), middlewareUtil and resources, and returns an Express-style handler (req, res, next). For a task, the function receives the workspace (the project's files), dependencies, options, taskUtil and log. Third, the project uses it: under server.customMiddleware with name, afterMiddleware or beforeMiddleware (where to place it), and configuration; or under builder.customTasks with afterTask or beforeTask. Many ready-made ones exist as npm packages, like ui5-middleware-livereload or ui5-tooling-transpile (used by this app).
keyPoints: A custom middleware runs in ui5 serve on each request; a custom task runs in ui5 build.
Declare it: kind: extension, type: server-middleware (or task), metadata.name, path to the implementation.
Middleware module: function({ log, options, middlewareUtil, resources }) returning (req, res, next) => {...}.
Use it in ui5.yaml: server.customMiddleware (afterMiddleware/beforeMiddleware, configuration) or builder.customTasks.

examples.title: A custom middleware in ui5.yaml
examples.code:
specVersion: "4.0"
metadata:
  name: my.app
type: application
server:
  customMiddleware:
    - name: add-version-header
      afterMiddleware: compression
      configuration:
        headerValue: "local"
---
specVersion: "4.0"
kind: extension
type: server-middleware
metadata:
  name: add-version-header
middleware:
  path: lib/addVersionHeader.js

questions.title: What was the deployment procedure to the SAP Cloud Platform (SAP BTP) Neo environment?
questions.description: Neo was SAP's original environment of the SAP Cloud Platform (today SAP Business Technology Platform, SAP BTP). It is a proprietary environment that SAP has announced to retire; new projects should use the Cloud Foundry (or ABAP) environment instead, and existing Neo apps are being migrated. You should still know how it worked, because older projects and documentation refer to it. A UI5 app on Neo was deployed as an HTML5 application. Its routing configuration was the neo-app.json file in the project root: it listed routes that map URL paths to destinations (named connections to back-end systems, maintained in the cockpit, often through the SAP Cloud Connector to an on-premise system) or to the UI5 runtime (like /resources served by the platform's SAPUI5 service). Deployment was typically done directly from the SAP Web IDE (Deploy to SAP Cloud Platform), or with an MTA archive and the Neo console client; each deployment created a new version, which then had to be activated in the cockpit. Apps were registered in the SAP Fiori launchpad of the Neo portal service. Many of these concepts (destinations, HTML5 apps, launchpad) continue in Cloud Foundry, with different tools. The steps were: build the app; configure neo-app.json; deploy it as an HTML5 application (Web IDE or the Neo console client, like neo deploy-mta); activate a version, because the app is not live until a version is activated; and register it in the launchpad site with a tile and a target mapping. Knowing the procedure is fine; recommending Neo for a new project is not.
keyPoints: Neo was SAP Cloud Platform's original, proprietary environment; SAP is retiring it in favor of Cloud Foundry.
UI5 apps were HTML5 applications with routes in neo-app.json (paths to destinations or the UI5 service).
Destinations (often via the Cloud Connector) connected the app to back-end systems.
Deployed from SAP Web IDE or as an MTA; each deployment was a version to activate in the cockpit.
Steps: build → neo-app.json → deploy → activate a version → register tile and target mapping. Never recommend Neo for new projects.

questions.title: What is the deployment procedure to SAP BTP, Cloud Foundry environment?
questions.description: On SAP BTP's Cloud Foundry environment, a UI5 app is usually deployed as part of a multi-target application (MTA). The project gets an mta.yaml file that describes its modules and the services they need. The UI5 app is built and zipped (an html5 module), and a deployer module uploads it into the HTML5 Application Repository, a BTP service that stores and serves the static files of UI apps. The app is reached through an application router: either the managed app router (provided by SAP Build Work Zone or the SAP Launchpad service) or your own standalone app router. The xs-app.json file in the app defines its routes: which paths go to destinations (named connections to back-end systems, defined in the destination service, possibly through the Cloud Connector), which go to the HTML5 repository, and which authentication is required. Authentication and authorization use the XSUAA service (with roles defined in xs-security.json). The steps are: build the MTA archive with the Cloud MTA Build Tool (mbt build creates an .mtar file), then deploy it with the Cloud Foundry CLI (cf deploy app.mtar), or let SAP Fiori tools do both (npm run build:mta and npm run deploy, set up with npx fiori add deploy-config cf). Finally, the app is added to the launchpad (SAP Build Work Zone) as a tile. The concepts to name: the app router is the single entry point; it authenticates the user, serves the static files from the HTML5 repository and proxies API calls through destinations, which makes everything same-origin, so there is no CORS. A destination is the configured connection to a back end, including its authentication, so the app never holds back-end credentials. The managed app router comes with SAP Build Work Zone; a standalone Node.js app router is used when you need custom logic in it.
keyPoints: The app is part of an MTA (mta.yaml); its zipped content is deployed to the HTML5 Application Repository.
An app router (managed via SAP Build Work Zone, or standalone) serves it; xs-app.json defines routes to destinations.
Destinations (destination service, Cloud Connector) reach the back end; XSUAA handles authentication and roles.
Build with mbt build (.mtar) and deploy with cf deploy, or use SAP Fiori tools' deploy configuration.
App router = single entry point and same-origin proxy (no CORS); destinations keep credentials out of the app.

examples.title: Build and deploy
examples.code:
npm install -g mbt
mbt build                         # creates mta_archives/my-app_1.0.0.mtar
cf login -a https://api.cf.eu10.hana.ondemand.com
cf deploy mta_archives/my-app_1.0.0.mtar

examples.title: A minimal mta.yaml for a UI5 app
examples.code:
ID: my.app
_schema-version: "3.2"
version: 1.0.0
modules:
  - name: myapp-ui
    type: html5
    path: .
    build-parameters:
      builder: custom
      commands: ["npm run build"]
      supported-platforms: []
  - name: myapp-ui-deployer
    type: com.sap.application.content
    path: .
    requires:
      - name: myapp-html5-repo-host
        parameters:
          content-target: true
    build-parameters:
      requires:
        - name: myapp-ui
          artifacts: ["myapp.zip"]
          target-path: resources/
resources:
  - name: myapp-html5-repo-host
    type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
    parameters:
      service: html5-apps-repo
      service-plan: app-host
  - name: myapp-uaa
    type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
    parameters:
      service: xsuaa
      service-plan: application
  - name: myapp-destination
    type: org.cloudfoundry.managed-service
    parameters:
      service: destination
      service-plan: lite

questions.title: How do you work with SAP Project Portal and Gerrit?
questions.description: Both are tools used inside SAP's development process; the exact procedures are company-internal and documented in internal wikis, so here is the general idea. SAP Project Portal is an internal tool where development projects are registered and their infrastructure is set up: for example the source code repositories, the build and CI configuration, and the people with access. Gerrit is an open-source, web-based code review tool for Git, which SAP has used widely. The key difference from pushing directly to a branch is that every commit is reviewed first. You clone the repository and install Gerrit's commit-msg hook, which adds a Change-Id line to each commit message; this ID links all versions of the same change. Instead of pushing to the branch, you push to a special ref: git push origin HEAD:refs/for/master. Gerrit creates a change for review. Reviewers comment and vote (for example Code-Review from -2 to +2), and the CI system builds and tests the change and votes on Verified. If you need to fix something, you amend the commit (keeping the same Change-Id) and push again, which creates a new patch set of the same change. When the change has the required votes (like +2 Code-Review and +1 Verified), it is submitted, which merges it into the branch. Many teams have moved to GitHub with pull requests, which follows the same review idea. The automatic verification usually builds the change, runs the unit and integration tests, checks coverage, and runs security scanning such as Checkmarx; a -2 Code-Review vote is a veto. The honest framing for a review: this is SAP-internal tooling and the screens differ per project; what matters is the concept that nothing reaches the main branch without an automated build, tests, a security scan and a human review, which is the same shape as a pull-request workflow on GitHub or Azure DevOps. Related: Nexus is an artifact repository, a private, controlled store for npm and Maven packages, so builds do not depend on the public internet and every dependency is approved and cached.
keyPoints: SAP Project Portal (internal) registers projects and sets up repositories, CI and access.
Gerrit: code review for Git; every commit is reviewed before it is merged.
The commit-msg hook adds a Change-Id; push to refs/for/<branch> to create a change; amend + push = new patch set.
Reviewers vote Code-Review (-2 to +2), CI votes Verified; with the required votes the change is submitted.
CI votes after build, tests, coverage and Checkmarx; -2 is a veto. Same idea as a GitHub pull request.
Nexus: a private artifact repository for approved npm/Maven packages.

examples.title: The Gerrit workflow
examples.code:
git clone ssh://user@gerrit.example.com:29418/my-app
# install the commit-msg hook so every commit gets a Change-Id
git commit -m "Add discount field"          # message ends with: Change-Id: I8f3c...
git push origin HEAD:refs/for/master         # creates a change for review

# review feedback: fix and update the same change
git commit --amend
git push origin HEAD:refs/for/master         # new patch set, same Change-Id
